awd_titl_txt: RAPID: Extensometers to Measure Afterslip on the Sagaing Fault Following the M7.7 March 2025 Mandalay Earthquake
awd_abstract_narration:
This project aims to measure ongoing slip along the Sagaing Fault in Myanmar, near and south of the epicenter of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck on March 28,2025, killing more than 3,600 people. While the fault near Mandalay slipped by about 15 feet (5 m), the southern end moved only a few feet. Thus, it remains unclear whether the southern segment is now locked or if it continues to slip slowly, raising concerns about future earthquakes near Yangon, a megacity of over 8 million residents.   Using highly sensitive instruments called creepmeters, the team will monitor surface fault movement with 1/10,000 inch (2.5 μm) precision, recording the information every minute. These measurements will help determine whether the fault is still moving silently (afterslip), which can precede future ruptures. A similar reduction in slip was seen during the 1906 San Andreas Fault earthquake, though such detailed monitoring was not possible then. Project data will help assess ongoing seismic hazard in one of Southeast Asia's most densely populated regions as well as to test instrumentation that may be used when similar type earthquakes occur in the U.S..

Following the Mw 7.7 Mandalay earthquake, segments of the Sagaing Fault are expected to be slipping slowly through the process of afterslip. This silent fault motion typically occurs near and beyond rupture terminations and may persist for over a year before decaying to negligible rates. Measuring the evolution of this slip will allow the team to assess how frictional properties of the fault were altered by the mainshock. An increase in slip rate may signal elevated seismic hazard, including the possibility of future triggered earthquakes.   The team will deploy highly sensitive creepmeters capable of resolving 2.5 μm to record fault motion continuously once-per-minute. These instruments can detect both dextral (horizontal) slip and fault dilation. Singapore-based collaborators, already active in Myanmar, will host and operate the devices as part of a new, instrument-based afterslip study.  This project focuses on the southern segment of the rupture, where slip during the earthquake was significantly less than further north. Southward propagation of afterslip into this area poses a direct threat to Yangon, a city of over 8 million. Unlike satellite-based geodetic methods, which offer only weekly resolution and far lower sensitivity, the ground-based data will provide high-resolution insight into near-field fault deformation.  This study will fill a critical observational gap in understanding the evolution of afterslip and its role in post-seismic hazard. It also provides a rare opportunity to study fault mechanics in near-real time, in a region of high vulnerability and limited prior instrumentation.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
In March 2025, a 475-km-long (295-mile) gently curved segment of the Sagaing Fault ruptured in a Mw 7.8 earthquake. Relative to Indochina, western Myanmar moved approximately 3.5 m northward along this curved fracture. The rupture propagated southward at about 6 km/s (13,400 mph), nearly twice the shear-wave velocity of intact rock. To place this in perspective, the rupture length is comparable to the distance between Los Angeles and San Francisco—a journey of about six hours by car, but only one minute for a rupture propagating along the San Andreas Fault.

This unusually high rupture speed is thought to be related to the absence of major bends and offsets along the fault, and some previous studies have described the rupture as being essentially free of such irregularities. We examined the smoothness of the rupture by calculating the best-fitting circle that approximates the mapped fault trace. To our surprise, the mapped rupture deviates from a circle centered south of Taiwan by, on average, less than 350 m - less than 0.1% of the 475-km rupture length (Figure 1).

The remarkable smoothness of the fault helps explain the rapid southward propagation of the rupture, but it also revealed something more important. The small departures from circularity were not random. Instead, they define long, straight fault segments joined by subtle bends or offsets from one another by several hundred metres

Security-camera footage recorded near the village of Thazi, about 100 miles south of the Mandalay epicentre, serendipitously captured slip on the fault during rupture. The two sides of the fault completed their relative displacement in only 1.3 s. After the earthquake, roads and footpaths at this location were found to be offset by approximately 2.5 m. This raised an important question: did slip cease immediately, or did fault movement continue after the initial rupture? 

In some major earthquakes, the fault indeed stops moving until the next earthquake hundreds of years later. However, preliminary satellite observations indicated that, at least locally, several centimetres of additional slip occurred during the week following the earthquake. We therefore rapidly designed, constructed, and shipped four sensitive instruments to Myanmar to record this continued movement. These extensometers measure fault displacement once every minute with a precision of about 2.5 μm (1/10,000 inch), have a measurement range of approximately 1.2 m (4 ft), and record fault motion in two horizontal directions, allowing sliding motion to be distinguished from opening across the fault. They operate for a year from flashlight batteries.

Although these displacements are small, the precision of the instruments allows the time history of afterslip to be reconstructed with remarkable accuracy. During the first few months, afterslip velocity decayed in a mathematically predictable manner before transitioning to a slower rate of decay. Most recently, the slip rate has increased slightly. Early in the record, slip velocity also increased following a magnitude 4.5 aftershock located about 7 km away. Perhaps the most surprising result is that surface slip appears to have begun several weeks after the mainshock, suggesting that the afterslip detected from satellite observations initially occurred at depth and only later propagated to the surface.

These observations indicate that stresses, frictional properties, and the subsurface distribution of slip had not fully adjusted more than a year after the earthquake. Such observations have rarely been obtained because they require rapid scientific response immediately following a major earthquake together with the availability of sensitive instrumentation. The measurements provide new insights into the physics of earthquake rupture and may ultimately contribute to improved forecasts of future earthquake behaviour. 

Apart from these exciting findings, the project must be considered a remarkable success in seamless international coordination.  Numerous stages of design, construction, shipping, international diplomacy, field planning and data retrieval were needed to capture the movements of the fault.  We are especially indebted to colleagues in Singapore whose long-standing collaborations with Myanmar scientists enabled the successful installation of the instruments. The extensometers were first shipped to Singapore for testing before being hand-carried to Myanmar, where local scientists and students selected installation sites, obtained permissions, and assembled the instruments across the surface rupture.  One Singapore colleague translated the installation manual from English into Burmese. Singapore and Myanmar funding sources purchased local construction materials and covered all local travel costs associated with the installations.

As a result of the project, research teams in both Singapore and Myanmar are now familiar with the instrumentation and methods required to measure afterslip and fault creep. In November 2025, the project supplied a second set of extensometers to Singapore that is being installed to continue these investigations and to expand the existing network.
